html:
A silver coin of standard weight issued by Sher Shah Suri, who ruled north India from 1540 to 1545. It is the direct ancestor of the rupee, still the name of the currency in India, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and other countries.

Sher Shah was an Afghan noble who drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India in 1540 and founded the short-lived Sur Empire. In five years he reformed the government, rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road, and reformed the coinage. Before him the currency was a mix of debased coins of different weights.

His system had three metals:

  • the silver rupiya, of about 11.5 grams of nearly pure silver,
  • the copper dam, used for daily buying and selling,
  • the gold mohur, for large payments.

The name comes from the Sanskrit rupya, meaning shaped or stamped silver.

When the Mughals returned in 1555, Akbar kept Sher Shah's coin, and the silver rupee became the money of the Mughal Empire. Silver from the Americas, paid by Europeans for Indian cloth, was melted down to make it. The East India Company later minted rupees too, and in 1835 it issued a uniform rupee for all of British India. The rupee also became the currency of the Persian Gulf, East Africa and Burma for long periods, carried there by Indian traders and British rule.
